在 2019年10月21日星期一 UTC+8上午12:35:16，Virgilio Gómez-Rubio写道：

> Hi,
>
> I do not this that this e-mail got a reply…
>
> > I found the estimation of  rho is significantly affected by the value of  beta1 and beta2 ，only in appropriate value the estimate works well.(eg: when set beta1=8,beta2=2,the result is very bad.) It puzzles me  cause I don‘t know how to choose appropriate value,it seems like I can only try different values blindly.I tried to find how people simulate data,all I found are real examples not simulations.
>
>
> I think that this happens because the variability in the covariates is larger than the one that you include in the random effects.
>
> > I am totally have no idea about this simple basic problem,it's very kind of you to help.There is my code,by the way,I'm worry about creating inappropriate spatial weight matrix so I use matrix in data(boston) instead.
>
> My advice is that you choose a different simulation study with a better balance between the fixed and random effects. For example, reduce the standard deviations of x1 and x2 to 1 and 2, respectively, This will reduce the variability in the fixed part of the model and will allow you to identify the fixed effects and spatial pattern better. See attached file.
>
> My feeling is that if you allow too much variability in the covariates this may confound with the smaller variability in the random effects, i.e., the model will not be able to tell whether the variability observed comes from the covariate or the random effect.
>
> Best,
>
> Virgilio

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Question about spatial regression with categorical confounders
messages.body_plain:
I would guess that you have no intercept in the model, and then
a factor would expand to all levels, like

> x = as.factor(1:4); y = as.numeric(x)
> model.matrix(y ~ -1 + x, data = data.frame(x,y))
  x1 x2 x3 x4
1  1  0  0  0
2  0  1  0  0
3  0  0  1  0
4  0  0  0  1
attr(,"assign")
[1] 1 1 1 1
attr(,"contrasts")
attr(,"contrasts")$x
[1] "contr.treatment"

but if you add the intercept, then the first level (by default) will be
set to zero

> model.matrix(y ~ 1 + x, data = data.frame(x,y))
  (Intercept) x2 x3 x4
1           1  0  0  0
2           1  1  0  0
3           1  0  1  0
4           1  0  0  1
attr(,"assign")
[1] 0 1 1 1
attr(,"contrasts")
attr(,"contrasts")$x
[1] "contr.treatment"

there is an entry about this, at the FAQ list at r-inla.org <http://r-inla.org>

H

messages.subject: LGCP optimization problem
messages.subject_clean: LGCP optimization problem
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am working on a model of sardine preferentially sampled data. I have followed the chapter 4 of the spde book and I have run a LGCP (Gamma-Poisson) model.

I have fitted a model with not shared smoothed bathymetry ("rw2) and another with just shared spatial effect and the results seem to be ok. However, when I run a model including the covariate (bathymetry) and the spatial effect the next error appears repeatedly:

file: smtp-taucs.c  hgid: 0bed76828f01  date: Tue Sep 03 11:21:49 2019 +0300
Function: GMRFLib_build_sparse_matrix_TAUCS(), Line: 758, Thread: 0
Variable evaluates to NAN or INF. idx=(2399,2399). I will try to fix it...

I saw on a post from some years ago that someone already had this problem and Haakon Bakka suggested it would need good priors to fix it. I have used pc.priors with a logic value for the range and I think it works fine when I look at the model hyperparameters output.

Despite of this, when I include the covariate the mentioned error appears and also the the corrected sd values are not good (eigenValues also quite  high):

Compute corrected stdev for theta[0]: negative 0.624263  positive 1.000000
Compute corrected stdev for theta[1]: negative 1.091022  positive 1.000000
Compute corrected stdev for theta[2]: negative 1.000000  positive 0.549892
Compute corrected stdev for theta[3]: negative 1.000000  positive 0.582806
Compute corrected stdev for theta[4]: negative 1.431875  positive 1.000000
Compute corrected stdev for theta[5]: negative 1.000000  positive 13.000841

I attach the code with some plots and the model result just in case it helps. I have also tried setting a prior for the covariate getting better values of the precision parameter but I must be missing something else.  If someone has a suggestion about what is happening or how could I improve the optimization process I would be very grateful.

Thanks in advance,

Fran

messages.body_plain:
Hi, I'm fitting a spatiotemporal model in INLA that runs fine on my Mac. However, I'd like to use the linux cluster at my institution for parallelization and higher memory.

The code runs without error on my Mac, but I get the following error coming from within inla.posterior.sample() on the linux cluster:

Error in inla.qsample(n = n.idx[k], Q = cs$config[[k]]$Q, mu = inla.ifelse(use.improved.mean,  :

  nrow(selection) == nrow(Q) is not TRUE

The code and data dependencies are large and complex so I will not share them here, but the main difference between the two running situations is:

1. Operating system (Mac vs Linux)

2. Needing to use INLA:::inla.dynload.workaround() on the Linux machine

Anything to point me in the right direction would be helpful. As of now, I'm having to fit the models on the cluster, transfer them to my machine, then sample from the posterior.

Thanks!

-Jessica Godwin

So, what's the difference between 'replicate' and grouping with 'iid'?

Thanks in advance for your helpful comments!
Minho

messages.body_plain:
The warning

file: smtp-taucs.c  hgid: 0bed76828f01  date: Tue Sep 03 11:21:49
> 2019 +0300
> Function: GMRFLib_build_sparse_matrix_TAUCS(), Line: 758, Thread: 0
> Variable evaluates to NAN or INF. idx=(2399,2399). I will try to fix
> it...
>

simply says that something (like the linear predictor) creates an
overflow (most likely), so something goes towards +/- infinity.
althrough there are steps taken to try to prevent this, it might not be
successful as in the case here.

Also

Compute corrected stdev for theta[0]: negative 0.624263  positive
1.000000
Compute corrected stdev for theta[1]: negative 1.091022  positive
1.000000

...

shows a bad sign, the corrections should in general be, one just below
1, and the other one, just above 1. if exactly eq to 1, its a bad sign
in the case that the estimate was to weird and it revert back to 1.

this mean that there is no good corresponance between the computed
Hessian and output of the correction procedure. It usually means, that
the mean is not accuractely enough located, which again might be due to
the problem above.

All of this, in most cases, are due to a to flexible model with not to
much information in the data. The data is what they are, so you may try
to tighten the model up with more informative priors to see what
happen.

If the problems comes because of an added covariate, then check that
the covariate is properly scaled, like x=scale(x), and set a very
informative prior for that coefficient. If 'x' confound to much with
the spde, you can constrain the spde to be orthogonal to that one, but
personally, I find this approach to be somewhat questionable.

Best
H

messages.subject: PIT for zeroinflatedpoisson0 data
messages.subject_clean: PIT for zeroinflatedpoisson0 data
messages.body_plain:
I have one question regarding PIT values for zeroinflatedpoisson0 data. I run the following code (which is taken from the examples) for the estimation of a zeroinflatedpoisson0 model and I ask for the estimation of the CPO and PIT values:

library(INLA)

n <- 1000
a <- 1
b <- 1
z <- rnorm(n)
eta <- a + b * z
p <- 0.2
E <- sample(c(1, 5, 10, 15), size = n, replace = TRUE)
lambda <- E * exp(eta)

y <- rpois(n, lambda = lambda)
is.zero <- (y == 0)
while (sum(is.zero) > 0) {
  y[is.zero] <- rpois(sum(is.zero), lambda[is.zero])
  is.zero <- (y == 0)
}

y[rbinom(n, size = 1, prob = p) == 1] <- 0

data <- list(y = y, z = z)
formula <- y ~ 1 + z
result0 <- inla(
  formula,
  family = "zeroinflatedpoisson0",
  data = data,
  E = E,
  control.compute = list(cpo = TRUE)
)

Then I checked and none of the observations presented a "failure" (i.e. sum(result0$cpo$failure) is equal to 0) and I created a plot for the PIT. This is the result:

I have a few questions here:

1) Since I am dealing with discrete data, the formula for the PITs should be: P(Y_i < y_i^obs | y_-i) + 0.5 P(Y_i = y_i^obs | y_-i), right?
2) Moreover, since these are zeroinflatedpoisson0 data, when y_i^obs = 0 then P(Y_i < y_i^obs | y_-i) = 0 and P(Y_i = y_i^obs | y_-i) is approximatively equal to "p" (I follow here the same parametrization as in INLA docs where p is the "zero-counts" probability, right? Then I would expect to see a lot of points around y = p/2 (i.e. 0.1), Why this does not occur?
3) Is it possible to modify the PITs values to take into account the "zero-inflation"? I think that, if the model is right (and this is the case), I should get a plot of uniform values between 0 and 1. I know that there is a paper on model assessment for count data (i.e. Predictive Model Assessment for Count Data, Czado et al., 2009) and I will read it tomorrow, but I was wondering if there is something focussed on zero-inflated count data.

Thank you very much for your help.
Andrea

messages.subject: calculating posterior lgcp likelihoods
messages.subject_clean: calculating posterior lgcp likelihoods
messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA community,

Hi, I am currently working on a LGCP problem,
and what I am trying to do is to evaluate likelihood of a point set conditional on the posterior lambda over a sphere (s^2) with radius 1.

According to Simpsons et al. (2016), log-likelihood of a LGCP is given as
log (\pi (Y | \lambda)) = |\Omega| - \int_{\Omega} \lambda(s) ds + \sum_{s_i \in Y} log(\lambda(s_i)),
where Y is a point set that I want to evaluate the likelihood at.

So I assume that |\Omega| is equivalent as area of the sphere, 4*pi*r^2, and I already know log lambdas as well.
The problem is when I need to integrate lambdas over the sphere.

Once again, according to Simpsons et al. (2016), we can calculate integration over the sphere by approximating
\int_{\Omega} \lambda(s) ds \approx \sum^p_{i = 1} \tilde{\alpha_i} \lambda(\tilde{s_i}).

Here, I need weights,\tilde{\alpha_i}, and I want to know how can I get these weights.
I suspect that these weights are areas for each node of the mesh, and therefore I might use
a <- diag(inla.mesh.fem(mesh, order=2)$c0)
is this right?

Overall, I have two questions
1. is there any error on the understanding of calculating likelihood?
2. how can I get weights alpha for integration?

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Specifying non informative priors for a binomial model INLA
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Specifying non informative priors for a binomial model INLA
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jonesmus,

INLA doesn't use sampling to make the inference, but instead numerical
optimisation and integration; the principle was introduced in the
theory was introduced in the Rue, Martino, Chopin (2009) JRSSB paper
"Approximate Bayesian inference for latent Gaussian models by using
integrated nested Laplace approximations":
https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-9868.2008.00700.x

As for "non informative" priors, that terminology is problematic,
since any prior can be said to be "informative" depending on what
parameter transformation/parameterisation it's specified for, and
depending on what the effect on the response variable distribution is.
Do you mean a "flat" prior for the Binomial(n,p) probability, or some
other prior?

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] extraconstr and observation matrices with rgeneric
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] extraconstr and observation matrices with rgeneric
messages.body_plain:
I'm not sure I get this right, but for a rgeneric model, x, you want to
condition on that x[1] = 0 ?

In that case, then can you do the conditioning yourself within the
rgeneric, as the prec matrix would be Q[2:n,2:n].

using constraints, saying that x[1] = 0, will make the posterior for
that node singular, a point mass at 0, which is not supported.

In case you fit the model, and then want to do the conditioning, its
possible to use inla.posterior.sample() for this, see the vignette

Conditional sampling from a fitted model - PDF  source  R code

in the package.

An alternative, is to condition on x[1]=0, almost, by forcing that one
to be close to 0, by introducting an 'observation' this is so, like a
Normal with mean x[1] and high fixed precision.

there is some issues about the normalizing constant for the conditional
distribution (on x[1]=0) being informative about some hyperparameters,
but this depends on which of the approaches above that is being used,
and also, if you see this as fitting a conditional model, compared to
doing conditioning in a fitted model.

Best
H

its a reasonable question and request. its notoriously difficult to do
well, however, due to the wide range of data types and ranges of
them...

what could been done, is to provide the posteriors for the linear
predictor eta_i | y_{-i}, and you could compute ynew_i|y_{-i} yourself
I guess more easily, or by simulations.

but for this to be useful in the context above, we would need

	eta_i | y_-i, theta         (*)

as the likelihood could depend on some of theta.

this one is computed, and used to compute the cpo values, but the
distribution itself it not stored.

its possible to compute this (*) yourself using the results in the
INLA-paper, and the implementation is nothing else than this.

let me know,
H

messages.body_plain:
Hi Thomas,

The case of constraining on individual nodes in SPDE models is best done by using the remaining sub graph Q, as discussed.  It’s a special case of a restriction of the degrees of freedom of the basis function space, that I partly implemented for 1D mesh/sde models, where one can set the boundary to be Dirichlet or Neumann, or free, which corresponds to keeping and/or modifying the boundary basis functions, and works both for degree 1 and degree 2 b-splines.  If there is broad usefulness of such a feature I can consider implementing that for 2d meshes in the future standalone fmesher package, which will likely handle things a bit more like PDE solver packages that define the function space that the solutions live on. That could then perhaps make such rgeneric models easier to implement.

Finn

messages.subject: Take multiple point sets into account for LGCP problem as input realizations
messages.subject_clean: Take multiple point sets into account for LGCP problem as input realizations
messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA community,

Hi, I am working on LGCP problems.
What I have is, I have multiple point sets, acquired from same space (which is actually brain),
so I can say that each point set (which is comprised of multiple points) is a realization of LGCP.

I am currently applying simple formula for estimation, form <- coordinates ~ 0 + intercept +  f(s, model = spde),
without taking different realizations into account, and I believe this overwhelmingly biases the estimation.

My guess is, to consider multiple point sets as multiple realizations,
I might use 'iid' random effects for each input? so that the formula could be
form <- coordinates ~ 0 + intercept +  f(s, model = spde) + f(set, model = "iid")

In this case, I am introducing a lot of parameters ( ~100 different point sets), and would it be okay?
Also, I am wondering how should I build a data stack to deal with it?
For example, let's assume that there are 3 points in addition to 100 meshes.

points <- data.frame(x = c(1, 0, 1), y = c(0, 0, 1), set = c(1, 1, 2))
nv <- 100 # number of meshes
n <- nrow(points) # number of points

Do I need to set 0 for mesh nodes?
stk.pp1 <- inla.stack(
  data = list(y = y.pp, e = e.pp),
  A = list(A.pp, 1),
  effects = list(list(s = 1:nv), list(intercept1 = rep(1, nv + n), set = c(rep(0, nv), points$set))))

Or do I need to set 1 for mesh nodes, and create multiple effects?
stk.pp2 <- inla.stack(
  data = list(y = y.pp, e = e.pp),
  A = list(A.pp, 1),
  effects = list(list(s = 1:nv), list(intercept1 = rep(1, nv + n), set1 = c(rep(1, nv), 1, 1, 0), set2 = c(rep(1, nv), 0, 0, 1))))

If I am wrong after all, what should I do to accomplish my goal?

In short,
To consider independent multiple point sets for LGCP problem, do I need to use `iid` random effects for each point set? If not, what should I do?
If I need to use `iid` random effects, how can I build the data stack, when considering `mesh`?

Thanks to your advices, I am advancing my research everyday.
I hope to introduce my work soon!

Yours Sincerely,
Minho

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Take multiple point sets into account for LGCP problem as input realizations
messages.body_plain:
Dear Minho,

Since you consider each data as replications of the same latent process, you can fit this considering the replicate argument in the f() function. Thus, your formula should looks lik e

  form <- y ~ 0 + intercept + f(s, model=spde, replicate=s.repl)

where the variable 's.repl' may be generated with the helper function inla.spde.make.index(), as

inla.spde.make.index(name='s', n.spde=spde$n.spde, n.repl=max(points$set))

The data projector matrix has to account for the replica as well, like

inla.spde.make.A(mesh=mesh, n.spde=spde$n.spde, repl=points$set)
best regards,

Elias

messages.body_plain:
Hi Minho,

What you describe as "iid" effects for "set" is almost equivalent to
having a separate intercept for each point set, but a common spatial
pattern; the relative point intensity between locations is the same
for all the sets, but the expected number of points is allowed to be
different. What Elias describes is a more general version, where the
entire spatial pattern is allowed to vary between the point sets. From
your problem description, having just separate intercept may be
enough, but we don't have enough problem insight to say for sure. For
the second type of model, you need enough data to be able to estimate
each intensity field; a nice feature is that it uses the same spatial
covariance parameters for each field, so that it borrows strength
across the point sets instead of trying to estimate completely
independent models.

To construct the stacks you probably need to think of the observation
likelihoods as one LGCP likelihood per point set. Since it's all
Poisson, you don't need to actually have "multiple likelihoods" in the
INLA sense, but thinking of it as multiple likelihoods may help in
figuring out how to make the stacks, and it seems that's the approach
your are already taking.  First of all, if you use f(set,
model="iid"), you really should have only one, common, intercept term
in the model, precisely as written in your "form", but your stack
constructions need some modifications.

It's not clear from you code if you're implementing it as
mesh-node-aggregated-counts, or as a direct continuous domain LGCP
likelihood. Since you don't mention integration weight, I'll assume
that you have discretised the counts around each mesh vertex, and are
using a direct Poisson count model based on that (the continuous LGCP
likelihood can also be done like this, but is a bit messier to do by
hand):

stk.pp1 <- inla.stack(
  data = list(y = y.pp1, e = e.pp),
  A = list(A.pp, 1),
  effects = list(list(s = 1:nv), list(intercept = rep(1, nv + n), set
= rep(1, nv + n)))
stk.pp2 <- inla.stack(
  data = list(y = y.pp2, e = e.pp),
  A = list(A.pp, 1),
  effects = list(list(s = 1:nv), list(intercept = rep(1, nv + n), set
= rep(2, nv + n)))
stk.pp.joint <- inla.stack(stk.pp1, stk.pp2)

If you can confirm precisely what likelihood you want to build, in
particular if you have aggregated counts, which your text seems to
indicate, but which doesn't seem to be the case in your code example,
since then each "point set" should have the same number of count
values. If you are instead working directly on the LGCP likelihood for
the point pattern, you will need to setup the two stacks for
point&integration instead of a regular Poisson likelihood, which is a
bit more involved, so I don't want to go into the details of that
until I know that's what you really need.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Dear Elias and Finn,

Thanks for your helpful comments.

>From Finn's description, what I need is to set up separate intercept for each set,
since eventually, what I want is to get a common spatial pattern across different realizations.

Below, I attached my typical implementation of the LGCP problem, following Krainski et al. (2018), without considering separate intercept for different sets,
and I guess I am implementing a direct continuous domain LGCP likelihood?

library(INLA)

# load point data
point <- readRDS("point.rds")

# build mesh and spde
mesh <- inla.mesh.create(globe = 25)
spde <- inla.spde2.matern(mesh)

nv <- mesh$n # number of vertices
n <- nrow(point) # number of points
n.repl = max(point$set)

iw <- inla.mesh.fem(mesh, order = 2)$va
imat <- Diagonal(nv, rep(1, nv))

y.pp <- rep(0:1, c(nv, n))
e.pp <- c(iw, rep(0, n))
lmat <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh = mesh, loc = point@coords)
A.pp <- rbind(imat, lmat)

stk.pp <- inla.stack(

  data = list(y = y.pp, e = e.pp),

  A = list(A.pp),
  effects = list(c(list(s = 1:nv), intercept = 1)),
  tag = 'pp.test')

form <- y ~ 0 + intercept + f(s, model=spde)

# data fitting
inla.setOption("num.threads", 6)
inla.setOption(pardiso.license = "~/pardiso.lic")
inla.setOption(mkl = TRUE)

pp.inla <- inla(form,
                family = 'poisson', data = inla.stack.data(stk.pp),
                control.predictor = list(A = inla.stack.A(stk.pp),
                                         compute = TRUE),
                E = inla.stack.data(stk.pp)$e,
                control.compute = list(openmp.strategy = "pardiso.parallel",
                                       dic = TRUE, cpo = TRUE, waic = TRUE, config = TRUE),
                control.inla = list(int.strategy = 'eb'),
                verbose = TRUE)

Please note that every set has different numbers of points. I attached the dataset as an example.

One concern is that I have many different sets eventually, and across different spatial patterns (some sets share different spatial patterns).
In other words, there are up to 73 sets, and some sets have points that have different spatial patterns (left and right brain).
For example, for left brain, there is interceptL and spatial pattern spL, while there is interceptR and spatial pattern spR.
When not considering sets, the formula would be
form <- ~ 0 + interceptL + f(spL, model = spde) + interceptR + f(spR, model = spde)
and if I consider sets, does it become as
form <- ~ 0 + interceptL + f(spL, model = spde) + interceptR + f(spR, model = spde) + set1 + set2 + ...  + set73 ?

Would it be possible to be dealt with INLA?
I have tried in INLA way recently, that I might stick to replicate, but if I do not need to, would I be able to implement this problem with "inlabru"?

In short,
What I want is to get a common spatial pattern across different realizations, with continuous LGCP likelihood.
I also need to consider that some sets contain points from different spatial patterns.
Can I do this with "inlabru"?
Many thanks,
Minho

> Hi Minho,

> What you describe as "iid" effects for "set" is almost equivalent to
> having a separate intercept for each point set, but a common spatial
> pattern; the relative point intensity between locations is the same
> for all the sets, but the expected number of points is allowed to be
> different. What Elias describes is a more general version, where the
> entire spatial pattern is allowed to vary between the point sets. From
> your problem description, having just separate intercept may be
> enough, but we don't have enough problem insight to say for sure. For
> the second type of model, you need enough data to be able to estimate
> each intensity field; a nice feature is that it uses the same spatial
> covariance parameters for each field, so that it borrows strength
> across the point sets instead of trying to estimate completely
> independent models.

> likelihoods as one LGCP likelihood per point set. Since it's all
> Poisson, you don't need to actually have "multiple likelihoods" in the
> INLA sense, but thinking of it as multiple likelihoods may help in
> figuring out how to make the stacks, and it seems that's the approach

> model="iid"), you really should have only one, common, intercept term

> constructions need some modifications.

> mesh-node-aggregated-counts, or as a direct continuous domain LGCP
> likelihood. Since you don't mention integration weight, I'll assume
> that you have discretised the counts around each mesh vertex, and are
> using a direct Poisson count model based on that (the continuous LGCP
> likelihood can also be done like this, but is a bit messier to do by
> hand):

>   data = list(y = y.pp1, e = e.pp),

>   effects = list(list(s = 1:nv), list(intercept = rep(1, nv + n), set
> = rep(2, nv + n)))

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

ok, just individual intercepts (instead of full individual fields) is
the version I gave, so just need to adapt it to the continuous LGCP
formulation you're using:

Build y.pp.1, e.pp.1, A.pp.1, etc for each set individually, just as
if you were only modelling one set.
Then build one stack for each set. To make the code more efficient, we
can store the yy.pp etc as a list, to not have to duplicate code:

# These lines should be replaced by some loop to construct the y,e,and
A information for each set and put directly in the common lists:
y.pp.list <- list(y.pp.1, y.pp.2, ...)
e.pp.list <- list(e.pp.1, e.pp.2, ...)
A.pp.list <- list(A.pp.1, A.pp.2, ...)

# Build the stack for each point set:
stk.pp.list <- lapply(seq_along(y.pp.list),
  function(set) {
   inla.stack(
     data = list(y = y.pp.list[[set]], e = e.pp.list[[set]]),
     A = list(A.pp.list[[set]], 1),
     effects = list(list(s = seq_len(spde$n.spde)),
        list(intercept = rep(1, length(y.pp.list[[set]]),
              set = rep(set, length(y.pp.list[[set]]))))
  }
# Merge the stacks:
stk.pp.joint <- do.call(inla.stack, stk.pp.list)

Then use the formula
   form <- y ~ 0 + intercept + f(s, model=spde) + f(set, model = "iid")
as you wrote before.

For your extended problem with two brain halves you can apply the same
technique; build each stack as if you only had one point pattern, then
combine the stacks.
I would suggest using model="iid" instead of the "fixed effect"
version of the set-specific intercepts, and definitely if you also
have common intercept terms (your interceptL and interceptR), since
that provides some shrinkage stability to the estimates, but if you
remove the common intercept terms, then your fixed effect intercept
approach should also work. The thing to watch out for is introducing
non-identifiability by having too many intercept terms for each set.

And yes, this should work in inlabru as well, and require less (none)
stack code,
but if you get it working in INLA now, then I recommend waiting a few
months to move to inlabru,
since I'm working on a major new release that will more consistently
support different INLA models.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Dear Finn,

Thank you for your invaluable advice.

I was having some time applying your advice to a partial data, and now I am getting results from the model using the full dataset!
I also look forward to the major update on the inlabru!

Many thanks,
Minho

On Friday, March 13, 2020 at 8:14:44 PM UTC+9, Finn Lindgren wrote:

> Hi,
>
> ok, just individual intercepts (instead of full individual fields) is
> the version I gave, so just need to adapt it to the continuous LGCP
> formulation you're using:
>
> Build y.pp.1, e.pp.1, A.pp.1, etc for each set individually, just as
> if you were only modelling one set.
> Then build one stack for each set. To make the code more efficient, we
> can store the yy.pp etc as a list, to not have to duplicate code:
>
> # These lines should be replaced by some loop to construct the y,e,and
> A information for each set and put directly in the common lists:
> y.pp.list <- list(y.pp.1, y.pp.2, ...)
> e.pp.list <- list(e.pp.1, e.pp.2, ...)
> A.pp.list <- list(A.pp.1, A.pp.2, ...)
>
> # Build the stack for each point set:
> stk.pp.list <- lapply(seq_along(y.pp.list),
>   function(set) {
>    inla.stack(
>      data = list(y = y.pp.list[[set]], e = e.pp.list[[set]]),
>      A = list(A.pp.list[[set]], 1),
>      effects = list(list(s = seq_len(spde$n.spde)),
>         list(intercept = rep(1, length(y.pp.list[[set]]),
>               set = rep(set, length(y.pp.list[[set]]))))
>   }
> # Merge the stacks:
> stk.pp.joint <- do.call(inla.stack, stk.pp.list)
>
> Then use the formula
>    form <- y ~ 0 + intercept + f(s, model=spde) + f(set, model = "iid")
> as you wrote before.
>
> For your extended problem with two brain halves you can apply the same
> technique; build each stack as if you only had one point pattern, then
> combine the stacks.
> I would suggest using model="iid" instead of the "fixed effect"
> version of the set-specific intercepts, and definitely if you also
> have common intercept terms (your interceptL and interceptR), since
> that provides some shrinkage stability to the estimates, but if you
> remove the common intercept terms, then your fixed effect intercept
> approach should also work. The thing to watch out for is introducing
> non-identifiability by having too many intercept terms for each set.
>
> And yes, this should work in inlabru as well, and require less (none)
> stack code,
> but if you get it working in INLA now, then I recommend waiting a few
> months to move to inlabru,
> since I'm working on a major new release that will more consistently
> support different INLA models.
>
> Finn
>
> On Fri, 13 Mar 2020 at 02:51, Minho Shin <mshin...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Dear Elias and Finn,
> >
> > Thanks for your helpful comments.
> >
> > From Finn's description, what I need is to set up separate intercept for each set,
> > since eventually, what I want is to get a common spatial pattern across different realizations.
> >
> > Below, I attached my typical implementation of the LGCP problem, following Krainski et al. (2018), without considering separate intercept for different sets,
> > and I guess I am implementing a direct continuous domain LGCP likelihood?
> >
> > library(INLA)
> >
> > # load point data
> > point <- readRDS("point.rds")
> >
> > # build mesh and spde
> > mesh <- inla.mesh.create(globe = 25)
> > spde <- inla.spde2.matern(mesh)
> >
> > nv <- mesh$n # number of vertices
> > n <- nrow(point) # number of points
> > n.repl = max(point$set)
> >
> >
> > iw <- inla.mesh.fem(mesh, order = 2)$va
> > imat <- Diagonal(nv, rep(1, nv))
> >
> > y.pp <- rep(0:1, c(nv, n))
> > e.pp <- c(iw, rep(0, n))
> > lmat <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh = mesh, loc = point@coords)
> > A.pp <- rbind(imat, lmat)
> >
> > stk.pp <- inla.stack(
> >   data = list(y = y.pp, e = e.pp),
> >   A = list(A.pp),
> >   effects = list(c(list(s = 1:nv), intercept = 1)),
> >   tag = 'pp.test')
> >
> > form <- y ~ 0 + intercept + f(s, model=spde)
> >
> >
> > # data fitting
> > inla.setOption("num.threads", 6)
> > inla.setOption(pardiso.license = "~/pardiso.lic")
> > inla.setOption(mkl = TRUE)
> >
> > pp.inla <- inla(form,
> >                 family = 'poisson', data = inla.stack.data(stk.pp),
> >                 control.predictor = list(A = inla.stack.A(stk.pp),
> >                                          compute = TRUE),
> >                 E = inla.stack.data(stk.pp)$e,
> >                 control.compute = list(openmp.strategy = "pardiso.parallel",
> >                                        dic = TRUE, cpo = TRUE, waic = TRUE, config = TRUE),
> >                 control.inla = list(int.strategy = 'eb'),
> >                 verbose = TRUE)
> >
> > Please note that every set has different numbers of points. I attached the dataset as an example.
> >
> > One concern is that I have many different sets eventually, and across different spatial patterns (some sets share different spatial patterns).
> > In other words, there are up to 73 sets, and some sets have points that have different spatial patterns (left and right brain).
> > For example, for left brain, there is interceptL and spatial pattern spL, while there is interceptR and spatial pattern spR.
> > When not considering sets, the formula would be
> > form <- ~ 0 + interceptL + f(spL, model = spde) + interceptR + f(spR, model = spde)
> > and if I consider sets, does it become as
> > form <- ~ 0 + interceptL + f(spL, model = spde) + interceptR + f(spR, model = spde) + set1 + set2 + ...  + set73 ?
> >
> > Would it be possible to be dealt with INLA?
> > I have tried in INLA way recently, that I might stick to replicate, but if I do not need to, would I be able to implement this problem with "inlabru"?
> >
> > In short,
> >
> > What I want is to get a common spatial pattern across different realizations, with continuous LGCP likelihood.
> > I also need to consider that some sets contain points from different spatial patterns.
> > Can I do this with "inlabru"?
> >
> > Many thanks,
> > Minho
> >
> >
> > 2020년 3월 13일 금요일 오전 6시 48분 12초 UTC+9, Finn Lindgren 님의 말:
> >>
> >> Hi Minho,
> >>
> >> What you describe as "iid" effects for "set" is almost equivalent to
> >> having a separate intercept for each point set, but a common spatial
> >> pattern; the relative point intensity between locations is the same
> >> for all the sets, but the expected number of points is allowed to be
> >> different. What Elias describes is a more general version, where the
> >> entire spatial pattern is allowed to vary between the point sets. From
> >> your problem description, having just separate intercept may be
> >> enough, but we don't have enough problem insight to say for sure. For
> >> the second type of model, you need enough data to be able to estimate
> >> each intensity field; a nice feature is that it uses the same spatial
> >> covariance parameters for each field, so that it borrows strength
> >> across the point sets instead of trying to estimate completely
> >> independent models.
> >>
> >> To construct the stacks you probably need to think of the observation
> >> likelihoods as one LGCP likelihood per point set. Since it's all
> >> Poisson, you don't need to actually have "multiple likelihoods" in the
> >> INLA sense, but thinking of it as multiple likelihoods may help in
> >> figuring out how to make the stacks, and it seems that's the approach
> >> your are already taking.  First of all, if you use f(set,
> >> model="iid"), you really should have only one, common, intercept term
> >> in the model, precisely as written in your "form", but your stack
> >> constructions need some modifications.
> >>
> >> It's not clear from you code if you're implementing it as
> >> mesh-node-aggregated-counts, or as a direct continuous domain LGCP
> >> likelihood. Since you don't mention integration weight, I'll assume
> >> that you have discretised the counts around each mesh vertex, and are
> >> using a direct Poisson count model based on that (the continuous LGCP
> >> likelihood can also be done like this, but is a bit messier to do by
> >> hand):
> >>
> >> stk.pp1 <- inla.stack(
> >>   data = list(y = y.pp1, e = e.pp),
> >>   A = list(A.pp, 1),
> >>   effects = list(list(s = 1:nv), list(intercept = rep(1, nv + n), set
> >> = rep(1, nv + n)))
> >> stk.pp2 <- inla.stack(
> >>   data = list(y = y.pp2, e = e.pp),
> >>   A = list(A.pp, 1),
> >>   effects = list(list(s = 1:nv), list(intercept = rep(1, nv + n), set
> >> = rep(2, nv + n)))
> >> stk.pp.joint <- inla.stack(stk.pp1, stk.pp2)
> >>
> >> If you can confirm precisely what likelihood you want to build, in
> >> particular if you have aggregated counts, which your text seems to
> >> indicate, but which doesn't seem to be the case in your code example,
> >> since then each "point set" should have the same number of count
> >> values. If you are instead working directly on the LGCP likelihood for
> >> the point pattern, you will need to setup the two stacks for
> >> point&integration instead of a regular Poisson likelihood, which is a
> >> bit more involved, so I don't want to go into the details of that
> >> until I know that's what you really need.
> >>
> >> Finn
> >>
> >> On Thu, 12 Mar 2020 at 14:05, Elias T. Krainski <eliask...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >> >
> >> > Dear Minho,
> >> >
> >> > Since you consider each data as replications of the same latent process, you can fit this considering the replicate argument in the f() function. Thus, your formula should looks lik e
> >> >
> >> >   form <- y ~ 0 + intercept + f(s, model=spde, replicate=s.repl)
> >> >
> >> > where the variable 's.repl' may be generated with the helper function inla.spde.make.index(), as
> >> >
> >> > inla.spde.make.index(name='s', n.spde=spde$n.spde, n.repl=max(points$set))
> >> >
> >> > The data projector matrix has to account for the replica as well, like
> >> >
> >> > inla.spde.make.A(mesh=mesh, n.spde=spde$n.spde, repl=points$set)
> >> >
> >> > best regards,
> >> >
> >> > Elias
> >> >
> >> > On 12/03/2020 06:27, Minho Shin wrote:
> >> >
> >> > Dear INLA community,
> >> >
> >> > Hi, I am working on LGCP problems.
> >> > What I have is, I have multiple point sets, acquired from same space (which is actually brain),
> >> > so I can say that each point set (which is comprised of multiple points) is a realization of LGCP.
> >> >
> >> > I am currently applying simple formula for estimation, form <- coordinates ~ 0 + intercept +  f(s, model = spde),
> >> > without taking different realizations into account, and I believe this overwhelmingly biases the estimation.
> >> >
> >> > My guess is, to consider multiple point sets as multiple realizations,
> >> > I might use 'iid' random effects for each input? so that the formula could be
> >> > form <- coordinates ~ 0 + intercept +  f(s, model = spde) + f(set, model = "iid")
> >> >
> >> > In this case, I am introducing a lot of parameters ( ~100 different point sets), and would it be okay?
> >> > Also, I am wondering how should I build a data stack to deal with it?
> >> > For example, let's assume that there are 3 points in addition to 100 meshes.
> >> >
> >> > points <- data.frame(x = c(1, 0, 1), y = c(0, 0, 1), set = c(1, 1, 2))
> >> > nv <- 100 # number of meshes
> >> > n <- nrow(points) # number of points
> >> >
> >> > Do I need to set 0 for mesh nodes?
> >> > stk.pp1 <- inla.stack(
> >> >   data = list(y = y.pp, e = e.pp),
> >> >   A = list(A.pp, 1),
> >> >   effects = list(list(s = 1:nv), list(intercept1 = rep(1, nv + n), set = c(rep(0, nv), points$set))))
> >> >
> >> > Or do I need to set 1 for mesh nodes, and create multiple effects?
> >> > stk.pp2 <- inla.stack(
> >> >   data = list(y = y.pp, e = e.pp),
> >> >   A = list(A.pp, 1),
> >> >   effects = list(list(s = 1:nv), list(intercept1 = rep(1, nv + n), set1 = c(rep(1, nv), 1, 1, 0), set2 = c(rep(1, nv), 0, 0, 1))))
> >> >
> >> > If I am wrong after all, what should I do to accomplish my goal?
> >> >
> >> >
> >> > In short,
> >> >
> >> > To consider independent multiple point sets for LGCP problem, do I need to use `iid` random effects for each point set? If not, what should I do?
> >> > If I need to use `iid` random effects, how can I build the data stack, when considering `mesh`?
> >> >
> >> >
> >> > Thanks to your advices, I am advancing my research everyday.
> >> > I hope to introduce my work soon!
> >> >
> >> > Yours Sincerely,
> >> > Minho

messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA community,

Hi, I am extending my research to multi-type LGCP from previous question:

https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/r-inla-discussion-group/tyC4CK1pvQc

There are over 200 point sets, marked as type A or type B.

I want to predict where each point set belongs based on loocv.

However, it would be infeasible to perform exact loocv since each estimation process takes ~ 4hours.

Point sets can be grouped by different sources (in the same space), but still we have to perform ~80 estimations.

Hopefully, a Bayesian Point Process Classifier has been proposed by Kang et al. (2014), which is based on importance sampling approach of loocv:

https://arxiv.org/abs/1412.1670

The probability that point set i belongs to type j (T_i = j) is given as

where p_j is prior probability of being type j and it is considered being equal for all types.

Therefore, we are basically classifying point set i by Q_hat, which is given as

where k = 1, …, K refers to K posterior simulations, and t_i refers to true type of point set i.

The problem is that I have approximated posteriors, while Kang et al. (2014) acquired samples form MCMC.

Is it a comparable approach to sample from approximate posteriors?

Another approach would be just use posterior mode \hat{\theta}.

In this regard, I approached both ways, and there are huge discrepancies between the two likelihoods.
\pi(x_i | T_i = j, \hat{\theta})
1/K * \sum_{k=1}^K \pi(x_i | T_i = j, \theta^(K))

where simplified \lambda_j = exp(intercept + f(s, model = spde)).

When I plug in likelihood 1 to the classifier, I get somewhat biased, but reasonable overall prediction accuracy ~77%, while the classifier only sticks to type A all the time, when I plugin the likelihood 2.

It seems like the discrepancy comes from few extreme samples of the posterior samples.

In short,
Is it okay to use posterior samples from INLA instead of MCMC? or stick to posterior mode?
How can I deal with the discrepancy between likelihood conditional on posterior mode and expected likelihood from posterior samples?

It seems like Vehtari et al. (2014) have dealt with similar problems:

https://arxiv.org/abs/1412.7461

which seems to be implemented in the “loo” package,

but I have no idea whether it would be possible to apply it into my problem:

https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/loo/vignettes/loo2-large-data.html

messages.body_plain:
I'm attempting to use the output from a multiplicative Poisson space-time model to calculate the relative excess risk due to interaction (RERI). If RR10 is the risk of the outcome when X1=1 and X2=0, RR01 is the risk of outcome when X1=0 and X2=1, and RR11 is the risk of outcome when X1=1 and X2=1, then the RERI is RR11 - RR10 - RR01 + 1. It's a simple rescaling of the values.

While I can calculate this value from the posteriors, I'm unable to figure out how to get 95% CIs around the value. If you need me to simulate data, I could figure it out, but I'm really bad at it, so it would take me some time, so I'll try just putting my code and see if its sufficient to clarify the question.

Specifying the outcome and SMR and an interaction term:

y14 <- mydata14$drug_death
e14 <- as.numeric(mydata14$POP) * sum(y14)/sum(as.numeric(mydata14$POP))
mydata14$PO_supply_X_ineq <- mydata14$s.PO.supply*mydata$s.gini

My Formula (greatly simplified):

formula.nbin <- y14 ~ 1 + f(mydata14$ID, model = "bym", graph = Cnty3109.adj, constr = TRUE, scale.model = TRUE) +
                                                        mydata$s.gini +
                            mydata14$s.PO.supply +
                            mydata14$PO_supply_X_ineq

mod.p <- inla(formula.nbin, family = c("poisson"),
                    data=mydata14, E=e14,
                    control.compute = list(dic = TRUE, cpo = TRUE, config = TRUE),
                    control.inla=list(tolerance=1e-20, h=1e-6),
                    control.predictor = list(compute=TRUE) #estimate predicted values & their marginals
                    )

I'm able to compute the value I wish using this equation:

lc1.1 = exp(mod.p$summary.fixed["mydata14|S|PO_supply_X_ineq","0.5quant"] + mod.p$summary.fixed["mydata|S|s.gini","0.5quant"] + mod.p$summary.fixed["mydata14|S|s.PO.supply","0.5quant"]) - exp(mod.p$summary.fixed["mydata|S|s.gini","0.5quant"]) - exp(mod.p$summary.fixed["mydata14|S|s.PO.supply","0.5quant"]) + 1
print(c(lc1.1=lc1.1))

However, it just print the value, not 95% CIs. I've thought about using linear combination, but I don't know how this would be done.

Any ideas?

Thank you!

messages.body_plain:
Hi Sujit,

as Virgilio says, it's not immediately obvious how to fit this model,
but there is a reparameterisation trick that can work for models like
this:

First, define a model as
  theta ~ N(0, \infty)
  (y_i | theta, lambda) ~ N(theta, 1/lambda^2)
Then, introduce a dummy observation that links theta to its desired prior:
  (z | theta, lambda) ~ N(sqrt(m)*theta, 1/lambda^2)
where the dummy observation is set to
  z = -sqrt(m)*mu
Since both y_i and z have the same observation noise, the
z-"observation" can simply be added to the observation vector, and a
weight sqrt(m) used for that observation in the predictor (can be
setup with inla.stack(), but I think one can also rescale the variance
for that observation, as a shorter alternative).

If the y-observations weren't there, that would lead to
  (theta|z,lambda) ~ N(mu, 1/lambda^2)
as desired, since it's equivalent to
  theta = mu + e
where
  e ~ N(0,1/m/lambda^2)

Equivalently, theta ~ N(mu,\infty), z = 0, would give the same result.

To set this up practically, I think you need
  f(theta, model ="iid",
hyper=list(prec=list(fixed=TRUE,initial=SomeSmallValue))))
where SomeSmallValue is sufficiently small but positive approximation
of 1/\infty.

There are several variations for how to implement this trick.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Hi! I found an error using INLA for estimating a large zeroinflatedpoisson0 model which occurs only when computing the marginals for the linear predictor.

The following code should exhibit the problem.

# packages
library(INLA)

# data
my_data <- read.csv(
  file = url("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/agila5/INLA_tests/master/Q1/data.csv"),
  colClasses = c("integer", "character", "character", "numeric", "character")
)

# Mod1: Hurdle - Poisson model with no random effect. Takes approx 1.5 minutes
# but runs fine.
mod1 <- inla(
  formula = number_of_car_crashes ~ highway + lanes,
  family = "zeroinflatedpoisson0",
  data = my_data,
  E = highway_length,
  verbose = TRUE,
  control.inla = list(strategy = "gaussian"),
  control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE)
)
summary(mod1)

# The problem is here
# Mod2: The same as Mod1 but with an unstrucutred random component on the hours.

messages.subject: Interpreting random slopes across across spatial regions for specific covariate
messages.subject_clean: Interpreting random slopes across across spatial regions for specific covariate
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am studying the effect of biodiversity on forest drought resilience. I am interested in understanding how the effect of biodiversity on drought coupling varies spatially across ecoregions. So what I want is a biodiversity beta coefficient for each ecoregion. To do this I have added random slopes for biodiversity values grouped by ecoregion.
Following code I found online here is my model:

formula <- resilience ~ 1 + biodiversity +
  f(ID, model = 'bym', graph = Hadj) +
  f(ecoregion, biodiversity, model = "iid", graph= Hadj, constr=FALSE)

model <- inla(formula,  family = "gaussian",  data = as.data.frame(eco_scale_rast_sub), control.compute = list(cpo = T, dic = T, waic = T), control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE))

So my questions are
1. Does including the graph =Hadj within the random effect portion of the formula account for spatial autocorrelation within individual regions?
2. If I were doing this model in lme4, I would need to add the random slope and overall beta coefficient to get the coefficient for each region. Is there a similar transformation that needs to be made with INLA random slopes or can I interpret them as is?
3. If I am not interested in the overall coefficient, do I still include biodiversity outside of the random slope?

I'm really new to INLA, so any help is greatly appreciated! Thanks!

>   f(ID, model = 'bym', graph = Hadj) +
>   f(ecoregion, biodiversity, model = "iid", graph= Hadj,
> constr=FALSE)
>

> dic = T, waic = T), control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE))
>
> So my questions are
> 1. Does including the graph =Hadj within the random effect portion of
> the formula account for spatial autocorrelation within individual
> regions?

Hi.

no. you're using the model iid, and the graph=Hadj is not used in that
case.

If you want to catch some spatial autocorrelation defined by the graph,
you may do instead

 f(ecoregion, biodiversity, model = "besag", graph= Hadj,
	scale.model=TRUE, constr=FALSE)

I guess your covariate 'biodiversity' is centered, at least, and
better, scaled as well.

You'll have a problem with this model and the confounding with the  '+
biodiversity' term, which you can remove from the formula.

If you're just interested in the differences from the overall trend,
you can do keep biodiversity term and then use constr=TRUE instead
of FALSE.

you can check out

@Article{art653,
  author =       {M. {Franco-Villoria} and M. Ventrucci and H. Rue},
  title =        {Bayesian varying coefficient models using {PC}
priors},
  journal =      {Electronic Journal of Statistics},
  year =         2019,

if you want to see what kind of priors would be suitable in your case.

Best
H

On Tue, 2020-03-17 at 08:08 -0700, Minho Shin wrote:
> Dear INLA community,
>
>
>
> Hi, I am extending my research to multi-type LGCP from previous
> question:
>
> https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/r-inla-discussion-group/tyC4CK1pvQc
>
>
>
> There are over 200 point sets, marked as type A or type B.
>
> I want to predict where each point set belongs based on loocv.
>
>
>
> However, it would be infeasible to perform exact loocv since each
> estimation process takes ~ 4hours.
>
> Point sets can be grouped by different sources (in the same space),
> but still we have to perform ~80 estimations.
>
>
>
> Hopefully, a Bayesian Point Process Classifier has been proposed by
> Kang et al. (2014), which is based on importance sampling approach of
> loocv:
>
> https://arxiv.org/abs/1412.1670
>
> The probability that point set i belongs to type j (T_i = j) is given
> as
>
>
>

> where p_j is prior probability of being type j and it is considered
> being equal for all types.
>
>
>
>
>
> Therefore, we are basically classifying point set i by Q_hat, which
> is given as
>
>
>

> where k = 1, …, K refers to K posterior simulations, and t_i refers
> to true type of point set i.
>
>
>
>
>
> The problem is that I have approximated posteriors, while Kang et al.
> (2014) acquired samples form MCMC.
>
> Is it a comparable approach to sample from approximate posteriors?
>
> Another approach would be just use posterior mode \hat{\theta}.
>
>
>
> In this regard, I approached both ways, and there are huge
> discrepancies between the two likelihoods.
>
> \pi(x_i | T_i = j, \hat{\theta})
> 1/K * \sum_{k=1}^K \pi(x_i | T_i = j, \theta^(K))
>
>
> where simplified \lambda_j = exp(intercept + f(s, model = spde)).
>
>
>
> When I plug in likelihood 1 to the classifier, I get somewhat biased,
> but reasonable overall prediction accuracy ~77%, while the classifier
> only sticks to type A all the time, when I plugin the likelihood 2.
>
>
>
> It seems like the discrepancy comes from few extreme samples of the
> posterior samples.
>
>
>
> In short,
>
> Is it okay to use posterior samples from INLA instead of MCMC? or
> stick to posterior mode?
> How can I deal with the discrepancy between likelihood conditional on
> posterior mode and expected likelihood from posterior samples?
>
>
> It seems like Vehtari et al. (2014) have dealt with similar problems:
>
> https://arxiv.org/abs/1412.7461
>
> which seems to be implemented in the “loo” package,
>
> but I have no idea whether it would be possible to apply it into my
> problem:
>
> https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/loo/vignettes/loo2-large-data.html
>
>
>
>
>
>
>
>
>

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Error with large zeroinflatedpoisson0 model when computing marginals for linear predictor
messages.body_plain:
yes, shows typical signs of out of memory...

since you're using the type0 zero inflation, you may just as well, run
it on the y[y>0] part of data, using either the type0 zero inflation
with a fixed p. that would give the same. p is essentially
sum(y==0)/length(y), and this should solve your problems.

if you want a model for 'p' you can code this as two likelihoods, one
for p and one for y[y>0].

messages.subject: Questions/Thoughts on left-censored data
messages.subject_clean: Questions/Thoughts on left-censored data
messages.body_plain:
I am thinking about the appropriate models to use for my continuous data with a large number of non-detects (i.e. left-censored). No code yet to share.

There have been a couple of papers that utilize the hurdle model, with a binomial and gamma distribution. My question here: is there a particular reason why the gamma model is used as opposed to a Gaussian model? I'd assume a binomial + Gaussian hurdle model could be implemented in R-INLA.

Second, there is quite a bit of literature in the frequentist community and one paper (attached) on Bayesian methods where the likelihood is adjusted to account for left-censored data by using the CDF instead of the PDF for the censored observations (Eq 2 of the attached paper). Is there anything in INLA that would prevent one from re-writing the likelihood with CDFs for the censored observations.

Many thanks,

Kyle

messages.body_plain:
On Tuesday, 12 September 2017 13:38:48 UTC+1, Jouni Helske wrote:
> Hi,
>
> I am trying to reproduce the example 5.4 of the Rue&Martino&Chopin's JRSS paper about cancer incidence (the data seems to be available in INLA package).
>
> Before even trying to figure out how to actually code this up with INLA, I started to wonder how the joint prior precision matrix of the model is computed? In the paper it says that it has dimension of 216 × 15 + 1 = 3241, where 216 is the number of spatial districts, 15 is the number of age groups and 1 is the common intercept. Comparing this with the example in the INLA review paper on https://arxiv.org/pdf/1604.00860.pdf, I don't understand where does this come from? Based on the review paper and my initial intuition I would have assumed the dimensions to be something like 216 (spatial random effect) + 216 (smooth spatial effect) + 15 + 1. Is there some sort of nesting going on or what?

Hi,
I would also like to reproduce this example. As you mention the data is available in INLA via data("Cancer"). However I am not sure how to obtain the neighbourhood structure -- i.e. to what district do each of the 216 numbers correspond to? This is required for the ICAR spatial term.
Thanks,
Adam

messages.subject: Two-way functional anova with AR1 errors
messages.subject_clean: Two-way functional anova with AR1 errors
messages.body_plain:
I'm trying to build a two-way functional anova model with AR(1) errors, but the results of the model give me the impression that I've made a mistake somewhere in the process.

My data has the following form, measured at 30 second intervals:

      id    mu alpha   eps     y
   <int> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
 1     1     0    NA     0  37.6
 2     1    30    NA    30  38
 3     1    60    NA    60  38.4
 4     1    90    NA    90  38.5
 5     1   120    NA   120  38.6
 6     1   150    NA   150  38.6
...

 1   119  2250  2250  2250  40.8
 2   119  2280  2280  2280  41
 3   119  2310  2310  2310  41
 4   119  2340  2340  2340  41.2
 5   119  2370  2370  2370  41.3
 6   119  2400  2400  2400  41.2

where the data has been formatted for a two-way functional anova model with 'mu' as the baseline effect, 'alpha' a treatment effect, and 'eps' being used for the AR(1) error terms.

I fit a basic model with a random intercept:

formula_ar1 <- y ~ -1 +
    f(mu, model = "rw2", constr = FALSE, scale.model = TRUE) +
    f(alpha, model = "rw2", constr = FALSE, scale.model = TRUE) +
    f(id, model="iid")

and the results is:

                                 mean   sd q0.025 q0.5 q0.975 mode
SD for the Gaussian observations 2.84 0.00   2.83 2.84   2.84 2.84
SD for mu                        0.21 0.02   0.17 0.21   0.26 0.20
SD for alpha                     0.25 0.05   0.17 0.24   0.37 0.23
SD for id                        5.01 0.10   4.83 5.00   5.22 4.98

This checks out since the about 95% of the functional observations are typically within about 15 units of their estimated group mean. However, this model doesn't adequately model the time-series nature of each function and I think the group effects variances are too narrow as a result. To address this I let the error terms be modelled by an AR(1) process with the same parameters for each term:

The model I am fitting is:

  formula_ar1 <- y ~ -1 +
    f(mu, model = "rw2", constr = FALSE, scale.model = TRUE) +
    f(alpha, model = "rw2", constr = FALSE, scale.model = TRUE) +
    f(id, model="iid") +
    f(eps, model = "ar1", replicate = id)

  result_ar1 <- inla(formula = formula_ar1, data= data,
                        control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE),
                        control.compute = list(config=TRUE),
                        control.family = list(hyper = list(prec = list(initial= 15, fixed = TRUE))))

 The result for this model is:

             mean   sd q0.025 q0.5 q0.975 mode
SD for mu    0.31 0.04   0.24 0.30   0.39 0.30
SD for alpha 0.36 0.07   0.23 0.36   0.52 0.35
SD for id    0.01 0.01   0.00 0.01   0.03 0.01
SD for eps   6.83 0.39   6.25 6.77   7.74 6.53
Rho for eps  1.00 0.00   1.00 1.00   1.00 1.00

The estimated group effects are now wider, but the variance parameter of the AR(1) process seems far too large given that y changes very little between observations (The standard deviation of the first-order difference of y is around 1 or less for all observations). Indeed, the stationary standard deviation implied by these estimates is nearly 100 (Rho is around 0.997).

Hi,
I tried to run some time-varying coefficient models of this type:

v1<-inla(l1 ~ f(otacka.s1,sin1,model="rw1",constr=FALSE)+f(otacka.c1,cos1,model="rw1",constr=FALSE),
data=data[1:n,], family="gaussian",control.compute = list(config = TRUE,cpo = TRUE, dic = TRUE, waic = TRUE))

in a situation where n can be quite large.
I can run the model with no problems with n<-20000, but not much larger.

The error message that I read at the end  of the verbose outout is:
            Cutoff value to construct local neigborhood:     0.0001
        Log calculations:        OError in inla.inlaprogram.has.crashed() :
  The inla-program exited with an error. Unless you interupted it yourself, please rerun with verbose=TRUE and check the output carefully.
  If this does not help, please contact the developers at <he...@r-inla.org>.

is there any simple way how to change settings to be able to handle much larger n (so far, I experimented with control.inla(strategy= ) but with no success)?

In case that the answer is no, I was thinking about circumventing the problem by a simplifying approximation consisting of splitting the data into several small-enogh blocks (B1, B2, ... Bk) so that INLA wil run with no problems. Then run B1 data and use last mean values of otacka.s1 and otacka.c1 as the starting value for the corresponding rw1's in B2 etc.
Is there a way to specify the starting value for rw1 (or even for rw2, crw2)?

All the Best
 Marek Brabec

messages.body_plain:
Mathematically I am looking to recreate:

y_ij(t) = mu(t) + alpha_j(t) + epsilon_i(t)

where t = 0, 30, 60,...,  i = 1,...,119 denotes the functional observation and j = 1,2 are the two groups each could belong to. Here, mu(t) is the grand mean function, alpha_j(t) is the group effect function and epsilon_i(t) is the residual error function for the ith individual. I am using the baseline parameterization with alpha_1 = 0. These are estimated using a smoothing spline approach (RW2 priors)

In my model I want epsilon_i(t) to be the sum of a random intercept and an AR(1) process. Thus

epsilon_i(t) = b_i + err_i(t)

where b_i ~ Normal and err_i(t) ~ AR(1) for all i.

I hope this makes sense.

messages.subject: Re: Two-way functional anova with AR1 errors
messages.subject_clean: Two-way functional anova with AR1 errors
messages.body_plain:
Yes, I want to restart the AR(1) process with each functional observation.

I am embarrassed to say I misunderstood that the AR(1) process in INLA is parameterized by the marginal standard deviation of the whole process rather than the random noise standard deviation. In light of this, the model results always made sense, I was just interpreting them incorrectly. Thank you for your help in any case!

On Thursday, March 26, 2020 at 2:25:04 PM UTC-4, Peter Collins wrote:
> I'm trying to build a two-way functional anova model with AR(1) errors, but the results of the model give me the impression that I've made a mistake somewhere in the process.
>
> My data has the following form, measured at 30 second intervals:
>
>       id    mu alpha   eps     y
>    <int> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
>  1     1     0    NA     0  37.6
>  2     1    30    NA    30  38
>  3     1    60    NA    60  38.4
>  4     1    90    NA    90  38.5
>  5     1   120    NA   120  38.6
>  6     1   150    NA   150  38.6
> ...
>
>  1   119  2250  2250  2250  40.8
>  2   119  2280  2280  2280  41
>  3   119  2310  2310  2310  41
>  4   119  2340  2340  2340  41.2
>  5   119  2370  2370  2370  41.3
>  6   119  2400  2400  2400  41.2
>
> where the data has been formatted for a two-way functional anova model with 'mu' as the baseline effect, 'alpha' a treatment effect, and 'eps' being used for the AR(1) error terms.
>
> I fit a basic model with a random intercept:
>
> formula_ar1 <- y ~ -1 +
>     f(mu, model = "rw2", constr = FALSE, scale.model = TRUE) +
>     f(alpha, model = "rw2", constr = FALSE, scale.model = TRUE) +
>     f(id, model="iid")
>
> and the results is:
>
>                                  mean   sd q0.025 q0.5 q0.975 mode
> SD for the Gaussian observations 2.84 0.00   2.83 2.84   2.84 2.84
> SD for mu                        0.21 0.02   0.17 0.21   0.26 0.20
> SD for alpha                     0.25 0.05   0.17 0.24   0.37 0.23
> SD for id                        5.01 0.10   4.83 5.00   5.22 4.98
>
> This checks out since the about 95% of the functional observations are typically within about 15 units of their estimated group mean. However, this model doesn't adequately model the time-series nature of each function and I think the group effects variances are too narrow as a result. To address this I let the error terms be modelled by an AR(1) process with the same parameters for each term:
>
> The model I am fitting is:
>
>   formula_ar1 <- y ~ -1 +
>     f(mu, model = "rw2", constr = FALSE, scale.model = TRUE) +
>     f(alpha, model = "rw2", constr = FALSE, scale.model = TRUE) +
>     f(id, model="iid") +
>     f(eps, model = "ar1", replicate = id)
>
>   result_ar1 <- inla(formula = formula_ar1, data= data,
>                         control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE),
>                         control.compute = list(config=TRUE),
>                         control.family = list(hyper = list(prec = list(initial= 15, fixed = TRUE))))
>
>
>  The result for this model is:
>
>              mean   sd q0.025 q0.5 q0.975 mode
> SD for mu    0.31 0.04   0.24 0.30   0.39 0.30
> SD for alpha 0.36 0.07   0.23 0.36   0.52 0.35
> SD for id    0.01 0.01   0.00 0.01   0.03 0.01
> SD for eps   6.83 0.39   6.25 6.77   7.74 6.53
> Rho for eps  1.00 0.00   1.00 1.00   1.00 1.00
>
> The estimated group effects are now wider, but the variance parameter of the AR(1) process seems far too large given that y changes very little between observations (The standard deviation of the first-order difference of y is around 1 or less for all observations). Indeed, the stationary standard deviation implied by these estimates is nearly 100 (Rho is around 0.997).
>

messages.subject_clean: Non-integer counts for binomial model
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

Following a recent update to INLA, I started getting the following error message:

*** ERROR ***  INLA.Data1: BINOMIAL likelihood is defined on integers, but y[4] = 1.16298220095

I traced this to an update in VERSION 20.01.25: "Added a check that discrete observations are indeed integers, like for Poisson, Binomial, etc"

https://bitbucket.org/hrue/r-inla/src/d74b5207d5473e40c0d7d6092f6a525d83403e04/rinla/inst/NEWS.Rd#lines-112

We often use the binomial model to approximate the likelihood for survey weighted data (e.g. as outlined by Chen, Wakefield, Lumley: https://www.stat.washington.edu/sites/default/files/files/reports/2011/tr583.pdf)

I wanted to enquire the reason for this change, and whether it is possible for this to raise a warning rather than an error (as in glm())?

Many thanks,
Jeff

Hi & thanks for your email.

To input non-integer values into the Biomial, can, yes, be seen an
error or not, depending on the situation. In most cases it is an user-
error, and for that reason its now raise an error.

With the binomial as

{n \chose y} p^y * (1-p)^(n-y)

its kind of obvious how to use a non-integer for p^y and (1-p)... for
the normalizing constant its not so clear  (used for marginal
likelihood), should we use the Gamma function which generalize the
integer factorials?  if not, how about runding to 'nearest integer',
using floor(),round() etc... its all these small details.

well, if there should be a 'binomial' for continous response, I'm happy
to add that one under a spesific own name, so it can defined properly
and the user can know exactly what is going on.

If you send me the details, I can add a 'xbinomial' today, similar to
inla.doc("xpoisson")

Best
H

Thank you for the very fast reply.

The common application for us with this is approximating a likelihood for weighted complex survey data. In this case both the effective events and the effective sample size could be non-integer.

On a bit more of a search, I see that this question has also come up before on the listserv without conclusion:

https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/r-inla-discussion-group/k5KbmV3HKPU

Since gsl_sf_lnchoose_e() takes unsigned int arguments, the previous behaviour presumably would have been to take the floor?

Thanks,
Jeff

messages.subject: quantile regression
messages.subject_clean: quantile regression
messages.body_plain:
In books and articles, there are references to INLA being able to perform quantile regression, primarily through a “laplace” family. The Yue 2009 paper describes this as an approximation to the actual distribution but one with low error.  An ordinary double exponential would be fine but Yue references the family as involving the asymmetric laplace, which would be fine also.

I am not seeing any likelihood with this name in the package anymore or anything in the News file regarding its removal or renaming.  Is this family or some equivalent still available as an option?  I would like to perform quantile regression to the median.

Thank you,

Jonathan

messages.subject: Question ST Preferential sampling model
messages.subject_clean: Question ST Preferential sampling model
messages.body_plain:
Dear inla users,

I would like to fit a preferential sampling spatio-temporal model, because I have preferential fishing data and covariates for each month within the period 2011-2013.

My first step was to fit the preferential sampling spatial model from the Chapter 4.3 of the spde book for 1 year data. However, fitting a spatio-temporal model provides more variability than fitting just the spatial model in Chapter 4.3 ( for 1 year of data I was doing the mean of the 12 covariate rasters trough the whole year).

My second step has been to fit the LGCP spatio temporal model from the Chapter 8.3 of the spde book. Nevertheless, with this I am just modeling the the point pattern, but not the abundance (marks). For my next step, I would like to include the Gamma likelihood in order to fit a spatio-temporal Preferential Sampling model.

I would like to ask if someone knows about any code example for a "spatio-temporal Preferential sampling" model or how could I join the Gamma likelihood to the model in Chapter 8.3 (I tried to combine it with the model structure in Chapter 4.3 but the results were not good at all).

I would appreciate any sugestions or pieces of advice.

Thank you in advance,

Fran

messages.subject: outlier in fitted values?
messages.subject_clean: outlier in fitted values?
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,
I got an "outlier" in my fitted values.. Isn't that very strange?

I used a zeroinflatedpoisson:
M25zap <-  inla(eval(f25),
           family = "zeroinflatedpoisson0",
             data = inla.stack.data(Stk25),
           control.family = list(hyper=list(theta=list(initial=-1.6))),
           control.compute=list(openmp.strategy="pardiso.parallel",config=TRUE, dic=T, waic=T),
             control.inla = list(diagonal = 0.01, strategy = "gaussian", int.strategy = "eb"),
             control.predictor =list( A = inla.stack.A(Stk25)),
             verbose=TRUE)

fitted values:
FitIndex <- inla.stack.index(Stk25, tag="Fit")$data
mu25 <- M25zap$summary.fitted.values[FitIndex,"mean"]

Is there any explanation for having a such as strange fitted value? And any suggestion how to deal with it?
Thanks in advance, Bram Parmentier
